# Composition audit

Label transparency and electrolyte balance across 22 products.

## What the labels declare

| Electrolyte | Products declaring an amount | Share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sodium | 21 | 95% |
| Potassium | 21 | 95% |
| Magnesium | 13 | 59% |
| Calcium | 6 | 27% |
| Chloride | 8 | 36% |


Chloride is the clearest transparency gap: it is the second most abundant ion in sweat, yet most labels omit it. Magnesium and calcium are declared mainly by premium sticks that use them as marketing differentiators, at doses far below daily requirements.


## Sodium-to-potassium ratio

Mass ratio (Na:K) and molar ratio are both shown because physiology works in mmol. Sweat is sodium-dominant (roughly 40 mmol/L sodium against 4–8 mmol/L potassium, a molar ratio near 6:1); most electrolyte products are far more potassium-heavy than sweat. That is not dangerous for healthy kidneys, but it is not sweat replacement either.

## Carbohydrate concentration

Carbohydrate percentage is grams per 100 mL at the stated dilution. Sport-nutrition guidance puts optimal beverage carbohydrate at roughly 4–9% for simultaneous fueling and emptying; above ~8% solutions slow gastric emptying and can cause GI distress. Hypotonic drinks (<4%) hydrate best; concentrated sticks rely on the user adding water.

## Added sugar and non-nutritive sweeteners

15 of 22 products contain more than 0.5 g sugar per serving; 7 are effectively sugar-free. Sugar is not an impurity in a sports drink, at 30–90 g/h it is the performance ingredient. In a low-sodium, low-carbohydrate product it is mostly palatability and calories.

| Sweetener class | Products |
| --- | --- |
| Sugar | 5 |
| Stevia + sugar | 4 |
| Sucralose + ace-K | 4 |
| Stevia | 3 |
| None | 3 |
| Sucralose | 2 |
| Monk fruit + stevia | 1 |
